tip: Allen nhw = they could, from gallu (be able). Add ddim to make it negative: Allen nhw ddim = they couldn't.
Cyn means before and takes the verb-noun straight on: Cyn gwneud = before doing. No 'ing', just the base verb.
Ga i (may I have) softens the word after it: pwdin turns into bwdin. Ga i bwdin = can I have dessert.
The -wyd ending makes a past with no stated doer: Anfonwyd y llythyr = the letter was sent.
Welsh has no verb 'to have'. gan carries it: ganddyn nhw = they have. Does dim gardd ganddyn nhw = they have no garden.
To bring is dod â (come with), so it needs â: Ddaeth e ddim â'i gôt = he didn't bring his coat.
Past negatives often use gwneud (do) as a helper: Wnaeth e ddim mwynhau = he didn't enjoy. The main verb stays as the base mwynhau.
Want to do something is eisiau plus the verb-noun, with no word for 'to': Dw i eisiau dringo = I want to climb.
Dylen ni means we should (a form of dylwn). No 'yn' follows, the verb comes straight after: Dylen ni drio = we should try.
wedi before a verb makes the perfect, 'have done': wedi gorffen = have finished. Wrap it with ddim to negate.
Faswn i = I would, the conditional of bod. Add ddim for the negative: Faswn i ddim = I wouldn't.
The future bydd softens to fydd in negatives: Fydd dim cyfarfod = there won't be a meeting.
caf i means I will get, an irregular future of cael (to get, receive): Gobeithio y caf i = I hope I get.
Need to do something is angen plus the verb-noun, nothing between: Dw i angen prynu = I need to buy.
Rhaid i plus a person plus verb-noun means must: rhaid i fi orffwys = I must rest, literally 'necessity to me to rest'.
For going to a person, use at rather than i: at y deintydd = to the dentist. i is for places, at for people.
The linking word a (and) triggers aspirate mutation, adding an h-sound: croesawgar becomes chroesawgar after a.
yn meaning 'in' triggers nasal mutation and shifts to yng: Cymru becomes Nghymru, giving yng Nghymru = in Wales.
